node.label: Mariana Valverde
node.date_label: “The Struggles of the Immoral” (with Weir) 1988 · The Age of Light, Soap, and Water 1991 · “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” 1992 · Diseases of the Will 1998 · Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge 2003
node.description: A sociologist and criminologist, not a historian by training (PhD in social and political thought, York, 1982; University of Toronto Centre of Criminology from 1993); historians read her study of social purity in English Canada as a statement of moral regulation. The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) follows reformers who sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' and argues that their movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class'; her notes trace the term to Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch but 'restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity', and she held, as 'Foucault and his followers have pointed out', that 'the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'. In 1992 she endorsed Mitchell Dean's argument that classical liberalism was 'a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation' and faulted Jean-Marie Fecteau's account of relief institutions as means of class control as 'a rather functionalist formulation'. Historians used and contested the frame: Tina Loo asked that it 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance' (1992), Donald Wright found that the reformers' silent audiences gave 'the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (1995), and Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau wrote that she and Doug Owram 'have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from “progressive” currents of modern thought and social action' (1996). Later books turn to alcohol and the will (Diseases of the Will, 1998) and to law (Law's Dream of a Common Knowledge, 2003).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Mariana Valverde (b. 1955); “The Struggles of the Immoral: Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation” (with Lorna Weir, Resources for Feminist Research, 1988); “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” (Labour/Le Travail, 1990); The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991; reissued 2008 with a new introduction); “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Gender Conflicts (ed. with Franca Iacovetta, 1992); Studies in Moral Regulation (ed., 1994); “Deconstructive Marxism” (Labour/Le Travail, 1995); Diseases of the Will: Alcohol and the Dilemmas of Freedom (1998). After 2000: Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge (2003); “Introduction to the 2008 Edition” of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water. In-period readings: Loo, Dehli and McCormick (reviews, 1992); Wright (1995); Christie and Gauvreau (1996); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Hunt (1997, 1999).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-14: her review essays 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians' (1990) and 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State' (1992) in full, and 'Deconstructive Marxism' (1995) at pp. 329–332; four in-period reviews or review essays of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water in full (Loo 1992, Dehli 1992, McCormick 1992) or in their Valverde section (Wright 1995, pp. 122–126). The book itself is known here only through those reviewers' quotations and through search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, which keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text (checked: pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 match the 1992 reviewers' page references; the 1991 preface's p. 9 appears as p. ix). Christie and Gauvreau (1996), Strange and Loo (1997), Hunt (1999) and Diseases of the Will (1998) are known only through such snippets. 'The Struggles of the Immoral' (1988, with Lorna Weir) is unread. She is not presented as the originator of moral regulation: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits their theorization as 'influential here' while finding that it obscures 'the agencies of regulation internal to civil society'. She called herself a sociologist working between disciplines; Loo (1992) and Wright (1995) read her that way, and the 2008 introduction, a later reading, says that 'no history department in Canada would ever hire me'. The 2003 book is cited at title level only; the 2008 introduction is a later reading and carries no claim about the 1990s.

incident_edges.relationship: Moral regulation as the formation of ethical subjectivity, carried out by philanthropies, churches and professions as well as the state: social purity in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991–92; the 1988 article with Weir is listed but unread)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full: 'I have argued elsewhere that the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests', though 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); she credits Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch with pioneering 'the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities' (p. 217). The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) is known here through in-period reviewers' quotations and through Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 University of Toronto Press reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C; partial preview, page images not viewable here because the viewing limit was reached), which keep the 1991 pagination: reformers sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 17; quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 316); purity work 'was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17; quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124); the reform movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 15; Dehli, p. 318); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; snippet, the last clause also quoted by Dehli, p. 317); '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations' (p. 166, as quoted by Wright 1995, p. 124). Her notes, seen only as snippets, place the concept: in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured' (n. 34, p. 171); Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity' (p. 173). Note 33 (p. 171) cites the 1988 article with Lorna Weir, which is unread here. In-period reception by historians. Tina Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, pp. 277–279, read) calls the book 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279). Donald Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, pp. 122–126 read) calls it a 'much talked about treatise' by 'a sociologist' (p. 122) and its concept of 'slippages' among class, gender, sexuality and race her 'most original' contribution (p. 124). Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo's Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada (1997; Google Books snippets, pp. 5, 63) write that 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation' (p. 5) and cite 'Mariana Valverde and others' on prostitution as 'the social evil' (p. 63). Mary Louise Adams's 'In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario' (1994) is cited at title level only. In-period criticism. Loo finds the second argument, on philanthropy and the state, 'more asserted than proved' (p. 279). Kari Dehli (Historical Studies in Education, 1992, pp. 315–319, read) would draw 'not quite so sharply drawn' conclusions about state and civil society and finds that she moves 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319). Wright judges her claim that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' 'untenable' and finds 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" ... conspicuously silent', so that 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (pp. 125–126). Chris McCormick (Atlantis, 1992, pp. 123–125, read) asks how her interpretations are made and judges that a 'thorough' reading of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123), while agreeing that 'Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124). Sociologists reformulated the concept: Alan Hunt's 1997 abstract (read) treats moral regulation not as 'a specific moral arena' but as 'a component of all fields of social relations', a wider definition than hers; in Governing Morals (1999; snippets) he writes 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155). Dean (1994) and Ruonavaara (1997) are cited through their abstracts as on the moral_regulation node. A contribution, not a founding: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits them. Diseases of the Will (1998), on alcohol and the governance of the will, is title-level here (snippets only) and does not support this edge.

incident_edges.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.

incident_edges.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: The user kept them apart (2026-10-12): the framework is "a different project closer to history of capitalism". named_group_routes.relationship: Foucauldian analysis contributes to the concept of moral regulation and its governmentality reformulation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges. Valverde's own acknowledgement (checked 2026-10-14 for revision 1.136, in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination): 'Following but modifying Foucault's approach, I take the term "discourses" to refer not to language as separate from the real world but rather to organized sets of signifying practices' (preface, p. x) and 'as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; also quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 317). Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, p. 123, read) reads her as modifying 'Foucault's archaeology' with 'an important commitment to social agency'. Strange and Loo (1997, p. 5, snippet): 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation'. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

Those objections concern one book and are recorded on the edge from the mariana_valverde entry (revision 1.136); this field-level edge stays a comparison. Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. Comparison only.

named_group_routes.relationship: Scott's theory of gender is weighed in Canadian debates over discourse, experience and gender history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Valverde's 1990 review essay in Labour/Le Travail, read in full, treats Scott's Gender and the Politics of History (with Riley) as a key work in 'the controversy about discourse theory'. She notes that poststructuralism had a 'bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)' and that 'in Canada' the debate was posed as 'a yes-or-no question'. She concludes that Scott 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow'. Pierson's 1991 essay on Canadian women's history opens on the turn to deconstruction, with Scott's theorising of gender as its most acclaimed example (opening read). Reference lists show Scott cited by Linda Kealey (1992), Pierson (1992) and Parr's 1995 CHR essay on gender history (OpenAlex metadata; texts unread). Limits: the evidence shows engagement and debate, not adoption. Valverde is sympathetic but critical. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a Canadian critique of the linguistic turn, but its treatment of Scott was not checked here. The 1995–96 Left History exchange is title-level and is not evidence that names Scott. PhD context: 64 of 120 Canadian History PhDs citing Scott engage this field (53%, lift 2.12); 39 engage childhood and youth (lift 3.21), and 49 working-class history (lift 1.87).

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

named_group_routes.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.

named_group_routes.relationship: Laura Lee Downs charges that Scott’s poststructuralist gender severs experience and subjectivity from the agency of the oppressed and treats discourse as “text-writ-large”; Scott replies that Downs misreads theory, which “analyzes how knowledge is produced” (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from women's history, whose experience-and-agency tradition Downs defends. Downs (CSSH 35:2, 1993; p. 414 and the notes shown by the publisher read): Scott's book "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought"; "There is much to admire"; but it contains "a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history"; notes: "Scott treats discourse as text-writ-large". Scott's reply in the same issue (p. 438 read): "profound misapprehension"; "theory analyzes how knowledge is produced; theory does not produce either real life or practical politics." Distinct from Palmer (edge_920), Valverde (edge_967) and Canning (edge_702).

named_group_routes.relationship: Named critics within the debate beyond Palmer and Valverde, whose arrows exist: Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (1987); Sangster's objection to 'the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (2000); Eley and Nield's charge of an 'ungenerous critique' that allows 'either discourse … or materialist social history' (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Scott's reply (ILWCH 32, p. 42, existing reading) reports Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject'; Stansell's own p. 24 (existing reading) sides with Scott on poststructuralism while holding that social analysis of real women's activities is needed (editors' remarks, read). Sangster 2000 (read in full), pp. 157–158: the Canadian feminists kept 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy', 'unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157; her 'constructed as material' objection on the same page is aimed at Sewell, in Berlanstein's volume, not at Scott); 'The post-structuralist subject thus stands in direct contrast to the Thompsonian subject'. Eley and Nield's reply (2000, p. 83, read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history'. verification.note: Abstract read: the settler approach has much to offer, but across 500 years of invading Indigenous North America the settler variety dominates some periods and regions and fades in others. 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are other modes; extractivism has become predominant in recent decades. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.139 Allan Greer person entry (Érudit PDF served to an ordinary request; text layer; folios 61–79, notes 80–86). Based on a keynote address to the CHA annual meeting (first-page note). Passages used: settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians' but 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the hazard of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality, as though the settler-colonial condition had no discernible beginning and as if it could never end' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory. I personally think it has a great deal to offer anyone trying to understand the present and the past of a country such as Canada' (p. 63); historians 'need to take on board the critique of settler-national historiography sketched out by Wolfe and developed more fully by others such as Lorenzo Veracini' (p. 63); 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'My objective is to try to historicize settler colonialism' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' as 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); settler colonization 'emerged as an important independent force' only from the last quarter of the eighteenth century (p. 70); 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' and 'An order based on territorial dispossession is not, and never has been, normal, natural, and inevitable' (p. 79). The source's page range 61–86 includes the notes.
